title: Crystal Divider MicroSim
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Clocks and Watches with AI
description: Watch a 32,768 Hz quartz crystal get divided by two fifteen times into a 1 Hz tick, then see how a parts-per-million error makes a clock drift each day.

learningObjectives: Apply repeated division by two to find the frequency at any stage of a 32,768 Hz divider chain.
Explain why 15 divide-by-two stages turn a 32,768 Hz crystal into a 1 Hz tick.
Calculate the daily drift of a clock from its crystal error in parts per million.
prerequisites: Know that frequency is measured in hertz (repeats per second).
Be comfortable multiplying and dividing by powers of two.

accessibility.notes: Screen-reader description provided; all controls are standard HTML elements.

controls.label: Start / Pause
controls.description: Starts or pauses time. The MicroSim opens paused, so the button first reads Start.

controls.label: Reset
controls.description: Sets both clocks to 00:00:00 and returns to the paused opening state.

controls.label: Run one day
controls.description: Fast-forwards 86,400 seconds in about 3 seconds and reports the drift.

controls.label: Slow motion
controls.description: Runs time 4,096 times slower so the fast stages are visible.

controls.label: Crystal error (ppm)
controls.description: How fast the crystal runs, in parts per million.

keyQuestions: What is the frequency after 8 divide-by-two stages?
Why does a 32,768 Hz crystal need exactly 15 stages to reach 1 Hz?
How much does a 30 ppm clock drift in a week?
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a crystal is perfectly accurate. Every crystal has a small error measured in ppm.
Thinking drift is random. A crystal that runs fast gains time steadily, so drift adds up day after day.
Thinking the divider chain changes accuracy. Dividing by two keeps the same ppm error at every stage.
assessmentOpportunities: Students can state the frequency after any number of divide-by-two stages (for example, 32,768 Hz after 4 stages is 2,048 Hz).
Students can calculate drift per day from a ppm value, such as 20 ppm giving about 1.73 seconds per day.
Students can explain why 32,768 Hz was chosen: it is a power of two, so halving it 15 times lands exactly on 1 Hz.
pedagogical.interactionPattern: Parameter exploration with a run/pause simulation
